summary:
Daegu carries the most sustained municipal hostility to a public queer event in South Korea, justifying a −0.07 deviation below the national 0.71. City officials directly clashed with police as municipal workers attempted to prevent Daegu Queer Cultural Festival organisers from setting up at their Jung District venue; the PPP mayor is named as the driver of the obstruction. Police, however, intervened to stop the municipal workers—an institutional response that partly mitigates the threat.

The festival, the second-oldest in Korea (since June 2009), has run every year for 17 years 'without fail… as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics,' including 2025 ('We Will Not Be E(r)ased') and 2026 ('事必Q정'). This persistence signals that municipal obstruction is real but does not prevent the event, and that the recurring annual counter-mobilisation by a Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella (about 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches along a 450 m stretch, timed against the festival) creates a high-density confrontational environment for a visible trans visitor during festival season. Outside those specific dates, everyday street risk is comparatively low per the dossier.

Compared to Seoul (0.66): Daegu's hostility is narrower in geographic scale but more directly obstructive to a traveler attending a specific public event. Seoul's 1.1-million megarally is a broader climate signal; Daegu's pattern is a repeated, concentrated interference at one venue every year. Both cities share the PPP-mayor-and-Pride framing; Daegu edges lower because the obstruction targets the event itself rather than surrounding it.

sources.summary: Hankyoreh English edition (19 June 2023): Daegu city officials and municipal workers attempted to block the Daegu Queer Cultural Festival from setting up at its Jung District venue (17 June), citing a missing road-use permit; police moved to stop the obstruction and protect the lawful registered rally, and the confrontation ended when municipal workers withdrew at noon. More than 500 civil servants had been deployed for 'vicarious administrative execution'. Mayor Hong Joon-pyo (People Power Party) attacked the city police chief on Facebook for 'essentially hosting a party for queer people'; the article frames Seoul's plaza denial, Incheon's film-festival pressure and Daegu's venue obstruction as a common pattern of PPP mayors challenging LGBTQ events, with conservative mega-churches mobilising each election cycle.

Korea JoongAng Daily (2025): the Daegu Queer Culture Festival — begun June 2009 and second-oldest in Korea after Seoul — announced that year's event under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on Dongseong-ro's bus-only zone in central Daegu, saying it has taken place every year without fail for 17 years as resistance to hate and discriminatory politics despite interference; organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as affirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.

Kidok (Korean Christian daily, September 2025): a Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer' response to the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450 m stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans.

NOTE: cached page returned only site navigation and Korean boilerplate (article body not served to automated fetch); the underlying Sports Korea item (29 May 2025) covers the 2025 Daegu Queer Culture Festival route and venue plans — starting at Daegu's 2·28 Memorial Park and marching via Gyeongpung, Bongsan, Baneul-daeryeong and Jungang-ro.

tangentialFactors: The annual counter-mobilisation around the festival is explicitly organised against homosexuality (same-sex conduct) and 'sexual minorities' generally rather than trans status specifically - its effect on visitors is the confrontational street environment it creates, not any trans-targeted rule.
